title: Role of Heat Treatment Atmosphere on the Microstructure and Surface Morphology of DLP-Fabricated High-Entropy Alloy Components.

recollection.starting_material: Guess: Digital light processing (DLP) printed green bodies made from a UV-curable resin slurry loaded with equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor) high-entropy alloy powders, followed by staged debinding.
recollection.intervention: Guess: Post-print thermal debinding and sintering/heat treatment at ~1100–1200 °C for 1–2 h under different atmospheres (air, inert Ar, vacuum, Ar/H2, and N2) to study their effect on densification, microstructure, and surface morphology.
recollection.structure: Guess: In Ar/vacuum/H2, the bulk retained a single-phase FCC HEA with higher densification and smoother surfaces; H2 yielded the cleanest, least-oxidized surfaces. In N2, a thin surface nitrided layer (e.g., CrN/(Cr,Fe)2N) formed with fine precipitates near the surface while the bulk remained FCC. In air, a duplex structure developed with an external oxide scale (Cr2O3 and Mn-rich spinel) and internal oxidation, increased porosity at the surface, and roughened morphology. Relative density approached ~96–98% in Ar/H2, was slightly lower in vacuum depending on debinding, and dropped further in air due to oxidation-induced porosity; grain growth was most pronounced in inert/H2 conditions.
recollection.mechanism: Guess: Atmosphere controls oxygen and nitrogen activity during debinding/sintering. Air promotes selective oxidation of Cr/Mn to form protective but brittle oxide scales and internal oxides, roughening the surface and limiting neck growth. Nitrogen dissolves and forms nitrides (primarily CrN) at the surface and grain boundaries, increasing hardness via precipitation and interstitial strengthening but can roughen the surface slightly. Hydrogen reduces native and debinding-derived oxides and aids carbon removal, enhancing neck formation and densification, yielding smoother surfaces. Inert/vacuum minimize reactions, allowing single-phase FCC to persist with grain growth driven by reduced second-phase pinning.
recollection.results: Guess: Ar/H2 heat treatments yielded near-full density (≈96–98%) with low surface roughness (Ra ≈ 1–3 μm) and a single-phase FCC structure; air produced thicker oxide scales (≈1–5 μm), higher roughness (Ra ≈ 6–10 μm), and lower relative density (≈85–92%). N2 formed a thin nitrided layer (≈0.5–2 μm) that increased near-surface hardness by ~10–30% (e.g., from ~160–190 HV to ~220–260 HV) while the bulk remained FCC. H2 slightly reduced hardness due to grain coarsening but delivered the smoothest, cleanest surfaces and best densification; vacuum/inert showed intermediate behavior.

score.note: The recollection only generically identifies atmosphere-controlled debinding/sintering of DLP green bodies. It incorrectly substitutes a CoCrFeMnNi alloy, multiple Ar/H2/N2 atmospheres, and different temperatures/times for AlCrFeNiSi treated in air versus mechanically evacuated oxygen-deficient conditions for 24 h. The proposed FCC, nitride, oxide-scale, density, roughness, and hardness results are not reported. Only the broad idea that oxidation can inhibit neck growth/densification overlaps with the actual mechanism; all quantitative values miss the reported O/C contents, crack behavior, 1050 versus 1100 °C consolidation, and approximately 0.5–5.17 MPa strengths.
